video_title: Most Crypto Tokens Were Never Meant to Enrich You | Scott Melker
gist: Scott Melker (Wolf of All Streets) argues the ICO/TGE-era token model is structurally dead and that value now has to accrue to real earnings and utility (citing Hyperliquid's buybacks and Zcash's privacy narrative) rather than narrative-driven 100x speculation, while separately laying out why Robin Hood Chain's tokenized-stock UX, Circle's rate-sensitive USDC revenue, and the Trump/Hunter Biden memecoin grifts are the real swing factors for crypto's next 12-24 months.

themes.theme: Token Economics: From Narrative to Earnings

insights.claim: During the 2020-2021 ICO/TGE boom, VCs could get an early tranche (roughly 15-20%) of a token immediately at the token generation event and cash out for a 100x within weeks, before the project had shipped any product, which structurally incentivized dumping on retail rather than building.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Explains why early-stage token allocations without long vesting cliffs are a red flag for retail buyers; longer VC lockups/delayed vesting is now viewed as a necessary structural fix.
insights.quote: they could probably if this thing launched with enough hype, they could 100x on the first 20% that they took out and then forget they ever owned it and it was an investment they made a month ago.

insights.claim: In hindsight, roughly 99% of tokens issued in the last cycle did not need a token at all; the token existed purely as a fast fundraising mechanism disconnected from whether the underlying project needed one to function.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A useful filter for evaluating any new token launch: ask whether the product actually requires a token, or whether the token is just a capital-raising wrapper.
insights.quote: the reality, and I think this was the hardest realization, was that 99% of those didn't need a token, right?

insights.claim: The next crypto cycle will not repeat the 'throw a dart and any token goes up 100x' dynamic of prior cycles; going forward, token value will accrue specifically to projects with demonstrated utility and earnings rather than to assets simply because they are part of the crypto market or attached to a hot narrative.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Investors should shift screening criteria from narrative/TAM stories toward cash-flow and buyback/earnings-accrual metrics when picking altcoin exposure.
insights.quote: I don't think we'll be able to throw a dart and your token goes up 100x just just because it's part of the crypto market or is it assigned a narrative.

insights.claim: Hyperliquid is cited as a rare example of a token an investor can value like a business: it runs large buybacks funded by real platform revenue and usage, giving it an earnings-based valuation case rather than a purely speculative one.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A concrete template for the 'value accrues to utility' thesis -- look for tokens with visible buyback mechanics tied to real revenue, not just TVL or narrative.

insights.claim: Zcash is one of the few smaller-cap assets that has genuinely 'captured' a durable narrative -- privacy -- and re-rated sharply as a result, distinguishing it from the broader pool of altcoins that are down over 90% from their peaks.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Narrative capture (owning a clear, singular use-case category like privacy) is flagged as one of the few remaining paths for a smaller-cap token to outperform in this cycle.
insights.quote: Zcash has captured the privacy narrative and is has gone kind of wild.

insights.claim: XRP is the one asset Scott Melker says he would never touch again, framing it as the archetype of a project that raised billions of dollars and only later, after its founders were already billionaires, began building real utility -- the incentive order he considers backwards.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A direct, named negative view from a high-profile crypto commentator that can be weighed against consensus bullish XRP narratives (ETF flows, Ripple settlement optimism).
insights.quote: One coin you would never touch again. God, do I have to say it? XRP.

themes.theme: Bitcoin Cycle Read and Price Targets

insights.claim: Bitcoin market bottoms unfold in two sequential phases: first a 'price capitulation' where holders panic-sell on a crash, followed by a longer 'time-based capitulation' where price goes flat and boring for months and believers quietly give up, especially while other assets like AI stocks, gold and silver are rallying and pulling attention away.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for timing accumulation: the boring, low-attention sideways grind after a crash -- not the crash itself -- is typically the real bottoming phase to buy into.
insights.quote: you get the time based capitulation, which is you get there and then you stay really really boring for a very long time and the people who believe just start to give up

insights.claim: The bounce from the low-$60,000s to roughly $82,000 within about a week, accompanied by the largest liquidation of short positions in Bitcoin's history and a ~24% weekly move, is treated as strong confirmation that a bottoming process (not necessarily a full bull resumption) has occurred, even though the broader bear market isn't confirmed over.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A specific, dated technical/positioning signal (record short liquidation + 24% weekly move) that can be cross-checked against derivatives data as a bottom-confirmation marker.
insights.quote: you can't ignore the largest liquidation of shorts in history and a 24% move in a week and pretend it means nothing.

insights.claim: Scott Melker's price target for Bitcoin in the next cycle, if the traditional four-year cycle pattern still holds, is roughly $220,000-$250,000, meaningfully above the prior cycle's ~$126,000 all-time high.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A concrete, named price target to track against outcomes, offered with the caveat that his prior cycle's similar prediction ($200k+ for 2021) also missed.
insights.quote: I think into the 200s, 250

insights.claim: The prior cycle's top of $126,000 was a historically weak cycle in relative terms: it did not even double the previous all-time high, whereas past Bitcoin cycles typically saw 3.5x to 10x moves above the prior cycle's peak, a pattern break Scott Melker found surprising.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Evidence that Bitcoin's cycle amplitude is structurally compressing as the asset matures and institutionalizes, which argues against extrapolating historical multiple-based price targets forward unadjusted.
insights.quote: I was very surprised that 126,000 was the top of that cycle. Didn't even 2x the previous highs and we always saw at least three and a half, 7 10x, you know, previous cycle highs.

insights.claim: Scott Melker's own retail advice is to dollar-cost-average into Bitcoin and ignore short-term price action, treating any price in the $40,000-$80,000 range as a 'liquidation sale' relative to his multi-decade target; he personally kept buying manually all the way down through the $60,000s and would prefer a lower price to accumulate at than a higher one.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A behavioral anchor for long-horizon investors: reframe drawdowns as discount buying opportunities rather than danger signals, conditional on a genuine multi-year time horizon.
insights.quote: I just say dollar cost average Bitcoin and forget about it.

insights.claim: Circle's revenue model is fragile because roughly 90%+ of its revenue comes from investing the dollar reserves backing USDC into short-term Treasuries and cash; if interest rates fall back toward 1% or a zero-rate environment, that revenue effectively disappears entirely, unlike Tether, which faces the same exposure but isn't publicly accountable to shareholders for it.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Circle (CRCL) earnings are effectively a leveraged bet on short-term rates staying elevated; a Fed cutting cycle toward ZIRP is a direct structural threat to its reported revenue, independent of USDC market-cap growth.
insights.quote: let's say 90% plus of their revenue simply comes from custodying the dollars that back USDC, right?

insights.claim: Circle's ARC blockchain is best understood as a strategic hedge against its own rate-cut revenue risk -- it needs a second, transaction/blockchain-based revenue stream to replace the interest income that will erode as rates normalize down over time.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Frames ARC's success or failure as an existential business necessity for Circle, not just an optional growth initiative -- worth monitoring transaction volume/activity on ARC as a leading indicator for Circle's diversification.

insights.claim: Despite Coinbase recently renewing its revenue-sharing deal with Circle (in which Coinbase reportedly receives roughly half of USDC's reserve-interest revenue), Coinbase also just joined the Stripe-led 'Open USD' consortium (built on Stripe's Tempo blockchain), which is a direct competitor to USDC -- a live conflict-of-interest signal in the stablecoin space.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Coinbase hedging against its own Circle partnership by backing a rival stablecoin consortium suggests it sees USDC's dominance as not guaranteed -- worth watching for share shifts in stablecoin market cap toward Tempo-based issuance.
insights.quote: Coinbase also just joined the Open USD consortium, which is in direct competition to Circle.

insights.claim: The 'L1 war is over' claim (that Solana and Ethereum have won among existing general-purpose Layer-1s) is directionally correct but overstated, because new purpose-built chains like ARC (stablecoins) and Tempo (payments) can still succeed without displacing Ethereum or Solana, simply by capturing entirely new growth in stablecoins and payments; meanwhile most existing L1s and L2s are expected to become 'zombie chains' that fade away amid a now-excessive supply of blockspace.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Reframes the L1 investing question from 'which chain wins the general-purpose war' to 'which niche-purpose chain captures a specific new growth vertical' -- a different screening lens for new chain launches.
insights.quote: I think most layer ones become zombie chains and completely disappear. I think most layer 2s become zombie chains and completely disappear.

themes.theme: Robin Hood Chain and the Tokenized-RWA UX Unlock

insights.claim: Robin Hood Chain's real unlock is UX, not novelty: moving funds from a Robin Hood brokerage account into the Robin Hood Chain wallet is frictionless enough for a crypto-non-native user, and the platform packages a roughly 6-8% DeFi yield in a way that doesn't feel like taking on 'crypto risk' to its millions of non-crypto-native retail customers.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A mainstream brokerage successfully abstracting away DeFi's complexity for millions of non-native users is a bigger distribution risk/opportunity for incumbent crypto exchanges than any single token launch -- watch RH Chain wallet/DeFi deposit growth as an adoption proxy.
insights.quote: getting money from Robin Hood to Robin Hood chain, from the exchange to the wallet is simple enough that my mom could figure it out.

insights.claim: Scott Melker predicts Robin Hood Chain will rank as a top-five blockchain by activity within 12 months, rather than fading into a footnote like prior memecoin/hype cycles (DeFi Summer, NFTs, the Meta/metaverse boom).
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable 12-month forecast to revisit against on-chain activity/TVL league tables for Robin Hood Chain.
insights.quote: Top five chain.

insights.claim: Crypto portfolio construction is increasingly a 'barbell': serious institutional-grade assets (Bitcoin, and to a lesser degree Ethereum/Solana/Hyperliquid) on one side, pure speculation on the other, with a thin, largely ignored middle -- roughly tokens ranked 10 through 1,000 on CoinMarketCap -- that attracts little investor interest.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A practical portfolio-construction lens: avoid the mid-cap 'dead middle' of the market and concentrate either in top-tier institutional assets or in explicitly speculative, high-conviction plays.
insights.quote: Everything else in the middle is this skinny bar that nobody's interested in. Coins, you know, 10 through 1,000 on Coin Market Cap.

insights.claim: Trading volume and attention in crypto are highly nomadic -- the same pool of 'degen' traders rotates between whichever chain currently has hype (Solana, Base, Robin Hood Chain, soon ARC), so a chain's current dominance is not sticky; Base may be losing share right now, but Coinbase's crypto-native position means it shouldn't be counted out long-term.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Chain-level 'market share' narratives (e.g. 'Base stole the meme trade') should be treated as short-lived rotations rather than durable competitive shifts when sizing positions tied to a specific chain's momentum.
insights.quote: I think Bass might be struggling right now, but I wouldn't bet against Coinbase, right?

themes.theme: Crypto Politics: The Clarity Act and the Grift Overhang

insights.claim: The DTCC has discussed targeting the settlement of quadrillions of dollars in tokenized assets by 2027, illustrating how far institutional blockchain-settlement infrastructure plans have advanced even though the market price of crypto assets has not yet reflected that adoption.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A concrete institutional-adoption data point and timeline (2027) worth tracking as a catalyst, even though the speaker argues this specific type of adoption is not itself directly investable.

insights.claim: The most investable version of crypto's promise is not Wall Street adopting blockchain 'plumbing' (e.g., DTCC settling on-chain, or JP Morgan settling with Wells Fargo via tokenized deposits) -- that's just infrastructure replacement with no retail investment angle -- but financial inclusion: someone in a country with a hyperinflating currency gaining access, for the first time, to tokenized US equities and stablecoin savings alongside Bitcoin, all in one wallet.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Reframes where the real addressable-market growth in crypto sits: emerging-market retail access to tokenized US assets and stablecoin savings, not incremental efficiency gains inside existing Wall Street plumbing.
insights.quote: someone in a foreign country who has never had access to United States capital markets, who could never participate in the stock market, and can now go on any exchange they want and buy a real tokenized version of a share, and they can buy it with a stable coin that's not in their hyperinflating currency.

insights.claim: The Senate vote framed in the media as 'the Clarity Act vote' was actually only a procedural motion to allow debate on the bill, not a vote on final passage; conflating the two overstates how close the Clarity Act actually is to becoming law.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: A factual correction that matters for anyone trading prediction markets or crypto-policy-sensitive assets around Clarity Act headlines -- procedural votes and final-passage votes should not be conflated.
insights.quote: today is just a procedural vote. It's a motion. It's it's effectively a vote to decide whether it's worth debating and voting on the Clarity Act.

insights.claim: Even a Democratic senator personally opposed to the Clarity Act may still vote yes on the procedural motion, because the crypto lobby (e.g., Fairshake) is powerful enough that voting no risks millions of dollars in opposition spending against them in the midterms, and voting yes today keeps negotiations open without locking in a final position.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Highlights crypto Super PAC spending power as a real swing variable in legislative outcomes -- a factor to weight alongside stated party positions when handicapping crypto legislation.
insights.quote: I think any Democratic senator will think twice about voting no if they think that it's going to cause the political lobby and fair shake to spend millions of dollars against them in the midterms.

insights.claim: Even if the Clarity Act ultimately fails, pro-crypto regulators (SEC Chair Atkins and the CFTC's Celig) have already shown they will unilaterally reverse prior hostile rules -- such as SAB 121, which had barred large institutions from treating custodied crypto as an asset rather than a liability -- creating a favorable regulatory environment for roughly the next two to two and a half years, though such regulatory gains are more easily reversed by a future administration than legislation would be. Prediction markets were putting only about a 6% probability on the Clarity Act becoming law before the midterms.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Suggests crypto businesses should plan around a ~2-2.5 year favorable-but-reversible regulatory window via agency rulemaking rather than waiting on legislation, and treat Clarity Act 'passage' headlines skeptically given the ~6% market-implied odds.
insights.quote: I think prediction markets are putting that like 6% by the way to actually become law.

insights.claim: The Clarity Act is politically stuck largely because Democrats will not hand Trump a legislative win that could be read as legitimizing his and his family's crypto-related enrichment; the Trump/Melania memecoin launched three days before his inauguration (timed to avoid emoluments-clause restrictions that applied once he took office) and Hunter Biden's 'Laptop' memecoin -- which briefly reached a roughly $140 billion valuation on only about $50,000 of actual liquidity before collapsing about 99% -- are cited as the concrete grift examples poisoning the negotiations, particularly the unresolved ethics clause.
insights.speaker: Scott Melker
insights.so_what: Political-family memecoin grifts are directly and causally linked to stalled crypto market-structure legislation -- a concrete mechanism explaining regulatory overhang beyond generic 'partisan gridlock,' and a reason to expect the ethics clause to remain the key blocking issue.
insights.quote: Hunter Biden launched a token last week called Laptop given it was like kind of a paper pump, but it went to $140 billion.
